source.title: Optimization Hyper-parameter Laws for Large Language Models
source.authors: Xingyu Xie; Kuangyu Ding; Shuicheng Yan; Kim-Chuan Toh; Tianwen Wei

page_placements.theme: Schedules and normalization enable conditional trajectory prediction

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether a different, schedule-aware fitted law predicts final training loss on held-out and larger-scale configurations. It does not reproduce the original power-law fitting method.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses Kaplan and Hoffmann scaling laws and includes scaling-law-style baselines, but most reported results concern Opt-Laws, a different predictor. Results about schedule ranking within the training grid, divergence detection, continual-training rankings, and fine-tuning rankings are not catalogued unless they directly report cross-scale loss prediction. Cited findings from other work are not treated as results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study proposes Opt-Laws, a schedule-aware log-loss regression with power-law scale terms, and reports mainly its own predictor's accuracy against baselines. It does not test whether loss follows a power law in N, D or C. It does not test whether such a law extrapolates over orders of magnitude: the jump is from ≤1.9B to 4.05B total parameters, about 2x, and tokens go up to 300B. It finds no compute-optimal split. Its exponent-sensitivity results concern Opt-Laws' own exponents, not published scaling-law exponents. The extrapolation tables (Tables 2, 3 and 13) compare the authors' method with other predictors. They are therefore own-method performance, not a test of V2.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that SDE-motivated Opt-Laws predict final training loss and rank LR schedules well: 94% Top-2 on held-out runs, divergence F1=0.92, and best family identified in all 5 out-of-family groups. They report sub-0.5% error transferring to 4B/300B-token runs. They limit validation to MoE models up to 4B parameters and the tested schedule families. Note that the 'larger' runs are only about 2x the largest training-grid model.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a 15-feature, schedule-aware regression law motivated by SDE convergence and escape analysis, with fitted exponents and coefficients; it is not the original parameter/token/compute power-law fitting procedure. The study compares against a Chinchilla-style baseline but does not reproduce the original sources' experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction quality depends on schedule features and the scale-power exponent choice. The paper reports that schedule-dependent exponent perturbations tested in Table 11 leave Top-2 unchanged, while scale-power exponent 0.50 lowers Top-2 to 80%. Predictions are also evaluated across different token budgets, model sizes, and schedule families.

fits_no_version.finding: Final loss depends on LR schedule shape at small token budgets (3B), and the gap narrows at 10B and 100B. The gap closes more slowly for the larger 8×0.6B model (Fig. 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LR-schedule sensitivity of final pretraining loss shrinks with token budget but persists longer for larger models, qualifying Kaplan et al.'s finding that schedule matters little.

fits_no_version.finding: When fitted on a linear-schedule grid and applied to larger, schedule-varied runs, a simplified law with Chinchilla-style N/D terms gives 6.9–8.9% error. Schedule-aware Opt-Laws gives about 0.2% (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling-law-style loss predictors without schedule features extrapolate poorly when LR schedules vary across runs.

record.problems: The predictor is a different fitted law from the power laws in the claim. Reported extrapolation concerns training loss, not held-out cross-entropy; the authors state that training loss closely approximates validation loss under their one-epoch setting. Empirical validation is limited to the stated MoE sizes, data budgets, and schedule families. No error bars or confidence intervals are reported for the prediction errors.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 held-out-grid metrics and Tables 9–10 feature/decay ablations were not extracted: they primarily evaluate schedule ranking or feature choices within the training grid, not larger-run loss extrapolation. Figure 6 schedule-family loss comparisons and the continual-training/fine-tuning ranking tables were also left out because they report schedule effects or schedule rankings rather than the tested power-law scaling claim.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss versus N, D or C across orders of magnitude.
No original-form power law is fitted on small runs and extrapolated orders of magnitude; the extrapolation gap is about 2x in parameters.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count.
Continual training and fine-tuning are used only for schedule ranking; no power-law form is tested.
No comparison of published laws' exponents or splits, and no curvature analysis.

missing.what: Pure Chinchilla power-law baseline (A/N^α+B/D^β+E) fitted on the 7-block grid: held-out R² 0.988 and Rel.Err 1.28%, but Spearman −0.16 within blocks. This is a within-grid fit over only 4 sizes and 3 token budgets, so it is at most weak context for V1.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' classification and V2/V7 links are not supported: every result row is the authors' own schedule-aware predictor or its baselines. The 'partial' states on comparator rows have no baseline and no meaning relative to the claim. Training loss in one-epoch training is used as a proxy for held-out loss.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly test whether held-out pretraining loss follows power laws in parameter count, tokens, or compute when other factors are not bottlenecks.
Tests Opt-Laws, not power-law fits from the original sources. Reports training-loss predictions rather than held-out cross-entropy, and does not test arbitrary scale ranges or model families.
Does not find the loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation under fixed compute or compare how optimal parameter and token counts grow with compute.
Does not hold parameter count fixed while varying depth, width, or other architecture details to measure their effect on loss.
Continual training and fine-tuning are included as settings for schedule ranking, but the study does not test whether the same power-law form holds in these regimes or in other modalities.
Does not test downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.

Tests sensitivity of Opt-Laws prediction quality to selected exponents, but does not directly compare published scaling-law exponents, test compute-optimal splits, or show scale-loss curves bending away from a single power law.

rows.subject: 8×0.6B MoE
rows.size_stated: approximately 4B trainable parameters; Table 6 gives 4.05B total trainable parameters
rows.operation_detail: Applied Opt-Laws fitted on the small-scale training grid to a 300B-token single-phase schedule without re-fitting.
rows.measure: Predicted versus actual final training loss; reported relative prediction error
rows.note: Reported error: 0.04%. The predictor was fitted on the smaller training grid and applied without re-fitting.
rows.check: These are the study's own Opt-Laws predictions versus actual training loss (Table 2). The predictor is a 15-feature schedule-aware regression, not a power law in N/D/C. The scale gap is about 2x in parameters (1.90B to 4.05B), not orders of magnitude. This is own-method performance, not evidence on V2.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Opt-Laws extrapolation to 8×0.6B and 8×0.3B pretraining configurations at 100B–300B tokens
reader_labels.reason: The distinct Opt-Laws predictor, fitted on the small-scale grid without re-fitting, has reported mean relative errors of 0.1, 0.2, 0.2, and 0.2 across the Table 3 groups, with all Table 2 errors below 0.5% (r1–r10, r23–r26). This supports extrapolation by this alternative predictor, not the original power-law recipe.

reader_labels.reason: The simplified Chinchilla-scale comparator has mean relative errors of 6.9–8.9% by group, while the Tissue comparator has 9.7–11.3% and linear regression 44.7–63.8%; prediction quality here depends on including schedule-aware features (r11–r22).
